query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Switching to a coarser powder feedstock—specifically increasing the particle size distribution from 15–45 μm to approximately 45–75 μm—will improve the deposition efficiency during thermal-spray processing of FeCoNiCrAl bond coats, leading to a thicker deposit while maintaining microstructural integrity and minimal as‐sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl bond coats produced from a 15–45 μm powder feedstock that yield insufficient coating thickness with acceptable but suboptimal oxidation levels.
generation.intervention: Replace the standard 15–45 μm powder with a coarser feedstock having a particle size distribution of roughly 45–75 μm, without changing other thermal spray parameters.
generation.conditions: Under standard thermal-spray deposition conditions for thermal barrier coating systems, as used in aero-engine environments with controlled gas flows and temperature settings.
generation.structural_mediator: Larger powder particles form larger molten droplets with higher momentum and lower surface area-to-volume ratios, resulting in improved splat formation and reduced in-flight oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The increased mass per particle and lower relative surface area enhance deposition efficiency by promoting complete melting and robust bonding, which in turn facilitates a thicker build-up while limiting oxidation during flight.
generation.predicted_outcome: The bond coat deposited using the 45–75 μm feedstock is expected to achieve a significantly greater thickness compared to the baseline, while retaining similar microstructural integrity and low levels of oxide formation.
generation.baseline: Thermal-sprayed FeCoNiCrAl coatings using a 15–45 μm feedstock that consistently yield a thinner deposit.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to remain effective as long as the particle sizes do not exceed the optimal melting range—beyond which incomplete melting or splashing may occur—and the existing spray parameters are adequately tuned for the larger particles.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in thickness and potential minor variations in oxidation levels may depend on further optimization of the processing parameters and the exact powder size distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel thermal-spray depositions on identical substrates using two feedstock size distributions—one with the standard 15–45 μm powder and the other with a coarser 45–75 μm powder—while keeping all other parameters constant.
measurements: Microstructural integrity (examining splat formation and porosity via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating produced with the 45–75 μm feedstock does not show a statistically significant increase in thickness (e.g., at least a 20% improvement) or if it exhibits increased oxidation or degraded microstructural quality compared to the 15–45 μm baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Isothermal oxidation experiments allow one to determine the rate of growth of an oxide scale. This is a measure of the performance of an alloy but it is at best a poor yardstick. Oxidation resistance does not depend only on the rate at which an oxide scale thickens but must also consider the ability of the scale to resist the thermally induced stresses associated with cyclic behaviour. We plan to evaluate the latter for the alloy Nb1.3Si2.4Ti2.4Al3.5Hf0.4, as well as its CTE and mechanical properties. The microstructures and isothermal oxidation of other alumina scale forming alloys of the same alloy system will be discussed in future publication.

Isothermal oxidation is a measure of the performance of an alloy but it is at best a poor yardstick. Evaluation of oxidation resistance must also consider the ability of the scale to resist the thermally induced stresses associated with cyclic behaviour. First one would need to find out whether the alloy MG5 has good oxidation under cyclic conditions. Then, one would need (i) to select (a) a substrate alloy with inherent oxidation resistance and balance of mechanical properties, (b) a coating process and processing conditions to deposit a (single or multi-alloy) bond coat, (ii) to evaluate the oxidation of the substrate/BC system under (c) cyclic conditions, (iii) to get insight into the mechanism(s) of the interaction between the coating and the substrate and thus to assess (iv) the stability of the substrate/BC interface and (v) the contamination of the substrate by interstitials. It is hoped that the work presented in this paper will inspire new research on the development of coatings for Nb-silicide based alloys.

drafts.hypothesis: Switching to a feedstock with a larger average particle size (e.g., a distribution shifted from 15–45 μm to around 25–60 μm) will improve the deposition yield of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat, achieving the required coating thickness while preserving the integrity and minimal as‐sprayed oxidation.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited via thermal-spray from a 15–45 μm feedstock that currently yields insufficient thickness.
drafts.intervention: Replace the baseline feedstock with a powder having a larger average particle size (shift the distribution to approximately 25–60 μm).
drafts.conditions: The intervention will be applied during standard thermal-spray deposition (using current plasma torch settings and ambient processing atmosphere) and intended for subsequent use as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system under high-temperature service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Larger particles have a lower surface-to-volume ratio and higher momentum, which leads to improved in-flight melting and deposition efficiency while reducing the relative surface exposure that promotes oxidation.
drafts.mechanism: By employing larger particles, the mass flux per particle is increased and the deposition yield is enhanced. The reduced surface area relative to volume minimizes oxidation, allowing a thicker, high-integrity deposition without incurring additional oxidation penalties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Coatings produced with the larger feedstock are expected to achieve a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the baseline (15–45 μm) case, while maintaining low oxidation levels and microstructural integrity.
drafts.baseline: Thermal-sprayed coatings deposited using the 15–45 μm feedstock, which consistently fall short of the required thickness.
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected as long as the increased particle size does not exceed a threshold (beyond about 60 μm) where incomplete melting or adverse splashing might occur. Optimization of the size range is crucial to avoid compromising coating quality.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of depositions under identical plasma-spray parameters and substrate conditions. One set uses the baseline 15–45 μm feedstock and the other set uses a feedstock with a shifted size distribution (25–60 μm). Evaluate the as-sprayed coating thickness, oxidation content, and microstructural integrity.
measurements: Oxidation levels (using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy or similar techniques)
Microstructural assessment (via scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the coating deposited with the larger feedstock does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the baseline or if it shows increased oxidation or compromised integrity relative to the control.

drafts.hypothesis: Switching the feedstock to a larger particle size distribution (e.g., 45–75 μm) will enhance the deposition efficiency of the FeCoNiCrAl bond coat by increasing the mass and momentum of individual droplets, leading to a thicker coating with maintained microstructural integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation compared to the 15–45 μm baseline.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy feedstock in the 15–45 μm range, which currently produces an insufficient bond coat thickness.
drafts.intervention: Use a feedstock powder with a larger particle size distribution (approximately 45–75 μm) while tuning thermal spray parameters (e.g., torch thermal input) to fully melt the particles without excessive oxidation.
drafts.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition conducted under controlled atmospheric conditions (to minimize oxidation) with adjusted torch parameters suitable for larger particles; subsequent service conditions are those of a thermal barrier coating (TBC) system where mechanical integrity and oxidation resistance are critical.
drafts.structural_mediator: Larger particles carry more mass and momentum, which favors improved splat formation and deposition efficiency. With properly adjusted thermal input to ensure complete melting, these enhancements mediate the structural formation of a thicker, continuous coating while limiting thermal exposure that might lead to oxidation.
drafts.mechanism: Increasing the feedstock particle size leads to larger molten droplets impacting the substrate. The enhanced momentum and volume of these droplets result in improved deposition efficiency, increasing the overall thickness. With adjusted spray parameters, the risk of oxidation is minimized because the thermal exposure is optimized to achieve complete melting without prolonged high-temperature residence in oxidizing conditions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The coating deposited using the 45–75 μm feedstock will be significantly thicker than that from the 15–45 μm baseline while retaining comparable microstructural integrity and exhibiting minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
drafts.baseline: Thermal-spray deposition using a 15–45 μm feedstock which currently yields a bond coat that is too thin for proper application in TBC systems.
drafts.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention may be limited if the particle size exceeds the optimal melting range, potentially leading to incomplete melting or increased splashing, which could compromise coating uniformity and oxidation resistance. Torch parameter adjustments must be finely tuned to accommodate the larger feedstock.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a comparative thermal spray experiment where two sets of coatings are produced: one using the standard 15–45 μm feedstock and the other using the 45–75 μm feedstock. Ensure that the torch parameters are adjusted for the larger particles to achieve complete melting. Maintain identical atmospheric conditions for both sets.
measurements: Coating thickness (via cross-sectional microscopy or non-destructive thickness measurement)
Oxidation levels (using techniques such as XPS or EDS to quantify surface oxygen content)
Microstructural integrity (using SEM to evaluate splat formation and porosity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating produced with the larger (45–75 μm) feedstock does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thickness relative to the 15–45 μm baseline, or if it shows increased oxidation or degraded microstructural integrity, the hypothesis will be rejected.

drafts.hypothesis: Increasing the feedstock particle size range from 15–45 μm to a larger range (e.g., 40–75 μm) will improve the deposition efficiency of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat during thermal spraying, leading to a thicker as-sprayed coating while preserving its integrity and minimizing in-flight oxidation.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat produced from 15–45 μm feedstock that currently does not achieve the required coating thickness.
drafts.intervention: Use a feedstock powder with an increased particle size distribution (e.g., 40–75 μm) during thermal-spray deposition.
drafts.conditions: Maintain the same spray process parameters (e.g., spray distance, gas pressures, plasma temperature) and service conditions typical of a thermal barrier coating system in aero-engine environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: Denser, larger molten splats with reduced relative surface area exposure during flight, leading to lower oxidation and better mass transfer during deposition.
drafts.mechanism: Larger powder particles carry more mass per particle and have a lower surface-to-volume ratio, which can reduce the extent of in-flight oxidation; they also require a shorter residence time in the high-temperature zone to achieve complete melting. This leads to improved deposition efficiency and a thicker deposit without compromising the coating’s integrity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: A bond coat with a marked increase in thickness compared to the baseline (15–45 μm feedstock), exhibiting a microstructure similar to the conventional coating and similar or lower levels of as-sprayed oxidation.
drafts.baseline: The current bond coat, deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock under identical thermal-spray conditions, produces a thinner coating that does not meet the required thickness specification.
drafts.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is expected within standard thermal-spray parameters and service environments for aero-engine bond coats; extreme changes to spray energy, distance, or environmental oxygen concentration could alter the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform two sets of thermal-spray deposition experiments using identical process parameters. One set uses the standard 15–45 μm feedstock (baseline) and the other uses an enlarged feedstock size range (40–75 μm). Post-deposition, assess the coating thickness, microstructure, and oxidation levels via microscopy, XRD, and EDS analysis.
measurements: Phase identification and oxide content analysis (XRD, EDS)
Evaluation of splat morphology and integrity (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating resulting from the larger feedstock does not show a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the baseline, or if it exhibits increased oxidation or compromised structural integrity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Using a coarser powder feedstock—with a size distribution shifted from 15–45 μm to approximately 45–75 μm—increases the deposition efficiency and thereby the bond coat thickness while maintaining coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coats deposited using 15–45 μm feedstock that result in insufficient coating thickness.
drafts.intervention: Replace the standard powder with a coarser feedstock (45–75 μm) without altering other thermal-spray parameters.
drafts.conditions: Under thermal-spray deposition conditions typical for thermal barrier coating systems, operating in aero-engine environments that require high-temperature cyclic exposure with controlled gas flows and energy input.
drafts.structural_mediator: Enhanced splat formation from larger, well-molten particles that have a lower surface area-to-volume ratio, limiting in-flight oxidation.
drafts.mechanism: Larger particles carry greater mass per particle and absorb/dissipate heat more efficiently, leading to fuller melting and superior bonding. Their reduced specific surface minimizes oxidation during flight, ensuring that the deposited material builds up more effectively to the required thickness.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The bond coat will achieve a significantly greater thickness compared to deposits from 15–45 μm powders, while exhibiting similar or lower oxide content and preserving microstructural integrity.
drafts.baseline: The existing deposition using a 15–45 μm powder feedstock yields a bond coat with suboptimal thickness and an acceptable but not improved oxidation level.
drafts.boundary: This intervention remains effective as long as the increased powder size does not adversely affect splat flattening or produce excessive porosity and if the altered powder size still allows for complete melting under the established spray parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel thermal-spray depositions of the FeCoNiCrAl bond coat using two feedstock size distributions—one with the standard 15–45 μm range and the other with the modified 45–75 μm range—while keeping all other process parameters identical.
measurements: Measure coating thickness via cross-sectional optical/SEM microscopy.
Quantify in-flight oxidation by XRD/EDS analysis of oxide formation.
Characterize splat quality, porosity, and adhesion properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the use of the coarser (45–75 μm) powder does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (for example, at least a 20% improvement over the baseline) or if it leads to increased oxidation levels or other microstructural defects, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
